Plagiarism detection in source code remains a significant challenge for both academic and industrial environments. While numerous detection tools exist, the corresponding anti-plagiarism strategies are scarce. This paper introduces an anti-approach based on code routing, developed as part of a research project. The study outlines the rationale for the routing method, details its architecture, and evaluates its performance. The findings indicate that the proposed approach is effective and applicable.

This paper establishes theorems concerning the absolute convergence of Dirichlet series that are automorphic. These findings are derived by applying the theory of relative coefficients to the automorphic Dirichlet series.

We establish a metric equivalent of the Milnor--Schwarz theorem, demonstrating that any metric group possessing finite asymptotic dimension is coarsely equivalent to a nilpotent group of identical approximate subgroups. This result enables the derivation of several metric counterparts to established group-theoretical findings, specifically yielding proofs of the coarse finiteness properties of groups that are extensions involving polycyclic groups.

This paper introduces a novel framework for estimating log-concave densities. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on the Convex Optimization (CO) method, our framework is built upon the Frank-Wolfe (FW) algorithm. We demonstrate that the FW estimator is a concave likelihood maximizer and establish its consistency. Furthermore, we prove that the rate of convergence for the estimator's objective function matches the optimal rate for the $L_1$-distance of the density, with the corresponding algorithm achieving superior computational efficiency compared to CO-based methods. Numerical experiments further confirm the improved performance of our approach.

This study introduces an entropic sampling approach for granular matter, utilizing the Wang-Landau algorithm to generate microstates according to their volume distribution. We demonstrate that the resulting microstates accurately reflect the system's entropy as a function of volume, thereby enabling the determination of the system's equilibrium volume.

This paper examines a novel two-player game played on a graph $G=(V,E)$, designated as the Explorer-Director game. In this framework, the Explorer selects a vertex $v$ at the start, while the Director chooses a vertex $u$ from $V \setminus \{v\}$. The Explorer then traverses a path from $v$ to $u$, with the objective of minimizing the number of edges traversed. The Director's goal is to select a vertex $u$ such that the length of the shortest Explorer-Director path originating from any chosen start point $v$ is maximized. We define the Explorer-Director number of $G$, denoted $\xi(G)$, as the maximum of the shortest path distances between any vertex $v$ and the endpoint $u$ selected by the Director. We establish that for any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, the inequality $n/2 \le \xi(G) \le 2n/3$ holds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the upper bound of $2n/3$ is tight for all sufficiently large $n$.

This study examines the frequency-frequency correlations of spectral densities derived from stochastic Gaussian processes along a specific single trajectory. We demonstrate that for such processes, these spectral spectral densities adhere to a specific scaling law, with the scaling function determined by the process's stationary spectral density. Furthermore, we establish that the associated frequency-frequency correlations for these spectral densities are non-negative. These theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.

This study introduces a novel approach for deriving interaction solutions within (1+1)-dimensional higher-order Broer–Kaup systems. By applying the traveling wave transformation, the associated partial differential equations are converted into first-order ordinary differential equations. Subsequently, specific first-order autonomous ODEs are solved using the proposed method to generate interaction solutions. These solutions are utilized to analyze interactions between different types of waves, with a particular focus on the collision dynamics of lump waves and kink waves.

We establish the conservation of energy for weak solutions of the incompressible Euler equations by relying on an identity that expresses the work done by the pressure force as a function of vorticity. This approach offers an alternative to the conventional derivation based on the duality relation $\int p\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}\,dV = 0$.

VIRUP is a virtual reality platform designed to facilitate the visualization and analysis of astronomical data. It is built upon the Unity game engine and utilizes the WebXR API to enable seamless VR and AR experiences across both mobile and desktop devices. The system is designed to be agnostic regarding input methods, supporting controllers, hand tracking, and traditional mice. Data is streamed from the server to the client via WebSockets, while a suite of custom Unity tools allows users to define and execute their own server-side data processing pipelines. This architecture is highly flexible, allowing for the integration of diverse data formats and visualization techniques. We detail the system's core components, the WebXR implementation, and the available data processing tools. Furthermore, we present a case study demonstrating the platform's application in visualizing and analyzing data from the Gaia mission.

This paper introduces a children's data literacy space-themed educational game that utilizes a tangible interface to introduce key concepts. Designed for young learners, the game features a physical controller that employs a 3D printer to fabricate, allowing children to interact with data through direct tactile feedback. The research outlines the game's design process, including its educational content, narrative framework, and technical architecture. Additionally, it presents findings from a pilot study conducted with 24 children, offering insights into how the game effectively supports the development of data literacy skills.

Software Defined Networking (SDN) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in network management, offering a flexible, programmable, and centralized approach to network control. However, the extensive search space inherent in the vast number of possible network configurations renders the exhaustive analysis of all potential data-paths unfeasible. Consequently, there is a critical need to identify and analyze only the most frequently executed operational data-paths. This paper introduces a novel method for detecting these high-frequency paths by leveraging flow statistics gathered from SDN controllers. The proposed approach employs a data-flow analysis technique to pinpoint the most utilized routes, thereby enabling network operators to optimize resource allocation and enhance overall network performance.

Disentangled representations are crucial for downstream tasks, yet existing methods often fail to fully capture the intricate relationships between latent factors. To address this, we introduce a new framework that utilizes Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the interdependencies among these factors. By integrating GNNs with a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), we develop a weakly disentangled representation learning approach. This method employs a variational autoencoder to generate initial latent factors, which are then processed by a GNN to learn their relational structures. The GNN's output is used to refine the VAE's latent distribution, thereby enhancing the disentanglement quality. We validate this approach across multiple datasets, demonstrating that it surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques.

This study investigates the hydrodynamics and energy harvesting performance of two heaving oscillating foils within a tandem arrangement. The analysis employs a two-dimensional potential flow model, which incorporates both the wake-circulation effects and foil flexibility. The wake-circulation model utilizes a vortex sheet to represent trailing vorticity, while the flexible foil model is represented by a panel method. The interaction between the flexible foil and the wake-circulation is simulated using a boundary collocation method. The study examines the impact of varying the distance between foils, the vortex sheet's initial position, and the flexible foil's natural frequency on the wake dynamics and the resulting energy harvesting efficiency. The findings indicate that the flexible foil's natural frequency plays a pivotal role in determining the wake's evolution and the efficiency of energy capture.

We introduce a Bayesian framework designed to infer the real-time dynamics of quantum field theories by utilizing data derived from Euclidean correlation functions. This approach employs a Bayesian inversion of the Mellin transform to reconstruct the spectral density, which represents the QFT's energy eigenvalues. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by applying it to $1+1$ dimensional lattice QCD, specifically using a toy model of a free massive scalar field.

We introduce a novel approach for investigating charge tunneling dynamics between a quantum dot and a superconducting island. This setup employs a quantum dot positioned near a superconducting island, with the system's charge state monitored via a sensing gate. Our analysis demonstrates that the sensing gate's response is highly sensitive to the specific charge configurations of both the dot and the island. Furthermore, we show that this response can be utilized to determine the charge states of the island, thereby enabling the detection of charge tunneling events.

Drug discovery is a critical yet arduous process, often requiring years of research and millions of dollars in investment. While recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated the ability to generate novel drug candidates with specific target affinities, these models frequently struggle with synthesizability and lack interpretability. To address these challenges, we introduce a new energy-based model designed to synthesize drug molecules with target specificity. Our approach employs a hierarchical framework that integrates a generative model with a scoring function to ensure the produced molecules are both chemically valid and synthetically feasible. Furthermore, we have developed a novel scoring function specifically for assessing synthesizability. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing baselines in generating novel, target-specific drug candidates.

The Graph Rewriting Machine (GRM) is a computational model that operates by repeatedly applying graph rewriting rules. In this model, a graph is represented as a collection of nodes and edges, where each node and edge type corresponds to a specific rewriting rule. This approach allows the machine to explore various possible execution paths, each representing a distinct computation. In this paper, we introduce a novel variant of the GRM called the Dynamic Geometry of Interaction (DGI) machine. In the DGI model, a graph is represented as a collection of nodes and edges, where each node and edge type corresponds to a specific rewriting rule. This approach allows the machine to explore various possible execution paths, each representing a distinct computation. We present proper motion measurements for the outer regions of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) using the Vast Magellanic Clouds (VMC) survey. By analyzing 1,000 stars with a mean magnitude of $G \sim 18.5$ mag, we achieve a proper motion precision of 0.12 mas/yr. Our findings indicate that the outer LMC shares the same systemic proper motion as the inner LMC, with a difference of only 0.06 $\pm$ 0.12 mas/yr. This result supports the hypothesis that the LMC is a single, gravitationally bound system. Additionally, we observe a significant proper motion difference of $-0.42 \pm 0.12$ mas/yr between the LMC and the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), consistent with their distinct systemic motions. We also detect a localized proper motion anomaly in the LMC's outer regions, characterized by a $-0.22 \pm 0.12$ mas/yr shift. This anomaly is likely attributable to the LMC's recent gravitational interaction with the SMC.

Electricity theft detection within Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) networks is essential for utilities to safeguard their financial interests. This study introduces a deep learning-based approach that leverages Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) to identify electricity theft, specifically by utilizing the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture. The method is designed to handle both single and multi-step ahead prediction tasks. To optimize the model's performance, we employ a random search strategy to tune hyper-parameters, specifically adjusting the number of LSTM units and the sequence length. Experimental results indicate that this proposed method achieves a 98% accuracy rate in detecting electricity theft.

This study examines the topological attributes of surface graphs that are both tight and surface-like. We demonstrate that a tight surface graph $G$ is embedded in a tight surface if and only if it can be constructed inductively through a specific inductive framework. This constructive method is further shown to yield a unique characterization of such graphs. Additionally, we establish that tight surface graphs are closed under the operations of taking subgraphs and forming strong joins.

The lifetimes of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons have been measured using their decays into $\Lambda^{0}K^{+}$ and $\pi^{+}K^{0}_{s}$, respectively, based on $pp$ collision data with a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV and an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector. The resulting mean lifetimes are $\tau(\Omega^{0}_{c}) = 1.626 \pm 0.031$ ps and $\tau(\Xi^{0}_{c}) = 1.642 \pm 0.031$ ps. These values align with the predictions derived from the quark model.

This study introduces a similarity-constrained subspace clustering framework designed for unsupervised hyperspectral image classification. The proposed method integrates two key components: a similarity constraint that leverages spatial information to enhance clustering accuracy, and a subspace affinity matrix that captures spectral data. The core objective is to identify a suitable subspace for each spectral endmember, thereby enabling effective classification. To address the computational challenges associated with hyperspectral data, we implement a fast approximate nearest neighbor search to generate the similarity constraint. Furthermore, we develop a novel algorithm that combines the subspace clustering process with a graph Laplacian to ensure the classification results align with the inherent data structure. Theoretical analysis confirms that the proposed framework is convex and possesses a unique solution. Extensive experiments on three distinct hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Accurately forecasting Arctic sea ice evolution requires precise knowledge of snow accumulation and its impact on ice albedo. However, current models often fail to adequately represent snow's spatial variability, particularly the formation of dune-like structures. This study introduces a simplified model of snow dune formation that accounts for snow's rheological properties and the mechanical interaction between snow and ice. The model demonstrates that the snow layer behaves as a granular material capable of forming dune-like topography, with peak dune height determined by the balance between snow's yield stress and the wind's shear stress. This mechanism explains the observed spatial heterogeneity of snow on ice surfaces. Furthermore, the model predicts that the wavelength of these snow dunes is proportional to the ratio of the wind's shear stress to the snow's yield stress.

We investigate the scattering of ultracold atoms and molecules under dynamic magnetic fields, revealing that a rapidly oscillating field can selectively inhibit specific scattering channels. This phenomenon, known as the selective quantum Zeno effect, is achieved by driving the oscillation frequency above the energy gap between the initial and final states of a scattering channel. This approach offers a viable pathway for the selective control of scattering channels at higher temperatures, where traditional methods based on static magnetic fields fail.

This study introduces a generalized Ito-Langevin framework based on the nonextensive parameter $q$, which accommodates both standard Ito-Langeville equations (when $q=1$) and a nonextensive variant. We demonstrate that this framework ensures the consistency of probability density functions evolving according to the time-fractional telegrapher's equation. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the nonextensive Ito-Langeville equations and the free energy exchange process.

This study explores the dynamics of a two-dimensional nodal-line semimetal subjected to a spatially uniform, time-dependent modulation of the light field. We demonstrate that this modulation induces a transition from a nodal-line semimetal to a higher-order topological Weyl semimetal. The resulting Weyl nodes are characterized by a nontrivial higher-order topology, specifically featuring hinge states with a quantized Chern number of $\pm 1$. Furthermore, we establish that the number of these Weyl nodes is determined by the modulation frequency.

Distributed computing is a critical field in computer science, yet the absence of a decentralized, secure, and efficient framework for distributed computation remains a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce Marvel DC, a distributed computing protocol that leverages blockchain technology to ensure decentralized operation. This protocol is designed to be secure, decentralized, and efficient, with the specific goal of enabling a distributed, permissionless network to compute a function $f$ over a dataset $x$ without revealing the function itself or the data. We have developed a novel blockchain-based architecture that supports Marvel DC, which is both flexible and scalable. Furthermore, we have designed a robust incentive mechanism to ensure the protocol is incentive-compatible, truthful, and individually rational. We also provide a formal security analysis of Marvel DC, demonstrating that it is provably secure.

This paper introduces a reduced reference perceptual quality model for 3D point clouds, designed to evaluate the visual quality of compressed point clouds against their original forms. The approach involves generating a synthetic point cloud that mimics the visual characteristics of the original, followed by jointly down-sampling and compressing both the original and synthetic datasets. The resulting quality assessment is derived from the visual discrepancy between the original and the reconstructed versions. The authors demonstrate that this method is effective for guiding rate control in the OCT-ALF compression standard. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model exhibits strong alignment with human subjective evaluations.

This study examines the QCD phase diagram using the holographic principle, which involves mapping quark mesons onto holographic counterparts within a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter (AdS) space. The QCD phase transition is modeled as a transition in the holographic geometry, specifically a first-order change occurring at the critical temperature $T_c$. By analyzing the behavior of the holographic black hole horizon, we determine the QCD phase transition temperature. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of the quark meson mass across varying temperatures. The results indicate that the quark meson mass increases with rising temperatures, a trend that aligns with lattice QCD simulations.

The increasing prevalence of knee joint disorders and the growing demand for specialized care underscore the critical need for advanced diagnostic tools. While deep learning has shown promise in this area, its application to knee joint MRI analysis remains limited. This study introduces SB-SSL, a self-supervised learning framework designed to extract robust features from MRI slices for classifying knee abnormalities. The proposed method employs a novel slice-based self-supervised transformer architecture that utilizes a contrastive learning approach to generate feature representations. These representations are then fine-tuned using a fully connected classifier to categorize abnormalities. Experimental results indicate that SB-SSL outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, achieving an accuracy of 90.1% on the OAI-Vision dataset.

We introduce a new few-shot font generation framework that enables the rapid creation of custom fonts using only a small number of character samples. This approach leverages local style cues from these few examples to synthesize new characters. Our method utilizes a neural network to map the local styles of input characters into a latent space, allowing for the interpolation of styles between them. This process facilitates the production of characters in previously unseen scripts. We have implemented this system and evaluated it through a few-shot font generation challenge, where the task involved designing a font for a specific set of Greek letters based on a reference font provided in Cyrillic. Our experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully generates characters in unseen Greek alphabets that closely resemble the stylistic features of the provided Cyrillic reference font.

We investigate the torsional effects within an equilibrated thermal environment of an anomalous fluid, specifically at a non-zero chiral charge density. This analysis reveals that the torsion tensor induces non-zero values for the traceless part of the stress tensor, the spin density tensor, and the chiral magnetic and vortical tensors. These torsion-induced contributions are found to be linearly proportional to the torsion itself and the chiral charge density.

Adaptive streaming is a prevalent technology for delivering online video, yet it often fails to maximize user experience due to the lack of awareness regarding individual preferences and network dynamics. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for personalized Quality of Experience (QoE) enhancement in adaptive streaming. This approach leverages the concept of digital twins to model the interplay between network conditions and user preferences, thereby enabling the identification of an optimal video bitrate. The proposed solution employs a hybrid strategy that combines a reinforcement learning agent with a digital twin-based prediction model to determine the most suitable bitrate for each user. Extensive simulations demonstrate that this personalized QoE framework outperforms existing methods in terms of both subjective quality and objective metrics.

The KM3NeT project is dedicated to constructing a neutrino observatory in the Mediterranean Sea, with its ARCA phase set to begin operations in 2024. This installation will feature a vast, deep-sea array designed to detect Cherenkov light from cascades and tracks generated by high-energy neutrinos. This study details the reconstruction of double-cascade events, which arise when neutrinos with energies exceeding 100 TeV interact with water, producing hadronic showers followed by decays of neutral pions into gamma rays. We detail the methodology for identifying these double cascades and evaluate their performance using Monte Carlo simulations. The results indicate that the algorithm achieves a signal efficiency of 70% for events with a gap of 100 meters or less, while maintaining a background rejection rate of 99.9%.

This paper investigates the deterministic periodic nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring logarithmic dispersion, a model emerging from the deterministic limit of the stochastic nonlinear Schrödinger equation under small noise dispersion. Our analysis demonstrates that for log-dispersion variants of the defocusing and focusing cubic nonlinearities in one dimension, well-posedness holds in $H^s$ spaces for $s > 1/2$. Furthermore, we establish that the corresponding Cauchy problem for the defocusing and focusing cubic defocusing log-dispersion equations in two dimensions is globally well-posed within $H^s$ for $s \geq 0$.

This study examines a wireless network where a source node communicates with a destination across $K$ parallel links, aiming to deliver a message of size $P$ bits within a specific deadline $T$. The system must ensure a target reliability level, $\epsilon$, by guaranteeing successful delivery with a probability of at least $1-\epsilon$. The transmission strategy involves splitting the message into $N$ packets, each of size $P/N$ bits, which are then encoded using a linear code of rate $R = \log_2(2^P/N)$. The objective is to determine the minimum number of packets $N$ required to satisfy the deadline and reliability constraints. The analysis considers two scheduling policies: static scheduling, where the number of active links remains fixed, and dynamic scheduling, where the active set changes over time. The paper establishes both lower and upper bounds for $N$ under each policy. Furthermore, it demonstrates that dynamic scheduling yields a significantly smaller packet count compared to static scheduling, particularly in scenarios with unreliable links.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant (SNR) is situated in the Galactic Center, adjacent to the supermassive black hole Sgr A*. Its location and morphology suggest an origin tied to a supernova event that occurred in close proximity to the black hole. This study examines the most probable sites for such an explosion, specifically focusing on the Galactic Center's star clusters and the circumnuclear disk (CND). By analyzing the CND's stellar population, we identify a significant concentration of young, massive stars in the region. These stars are likely responsible for the CND's high density and are expected to undergo supernovae within the next 10 to 100 million years. Consequently, the CND is a prime candidate for producing the SNR Sgr A East.

The Standard Model (SM) is a highly successful framework that has been rigorously tested through numerous experiments. However, recent measurements of B meson decays have revealed significant anomalies, suggesting potential new physics beyond the SM. This review examines the current status of these deviations, focusing on the $R_{K^{(*)}}$ and $R_{D^{(*)}}$ ratios, which compare decay rates of $B$ mesons involving leptons of different flavors. We analyze the experimental data, theoretical predictions, and the implications of these discrepancies for identifying new particles. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings for the flavor structure of the SM and the nature of new physics.

This paper outlines the methodology and system developed by the DisCoDisCo team for the DISRPT2021 shared task, which focuses on discourse segmentation, classification, and connective detection. The system employs a two-stage approach: first, a conditional random field (CRF) model segments the text into discourse units (DUs); second, a transformer-based architecture classifies these units. To enhance performance, the training data was augmented with additional annotations for discourse priming and discourse coherence. The system achieved an F1 score of 79.4 on the segmentation task and 75.4 on the classification task, surpassing the results of the system developed by the task organizers.

The advent of 6G and subsequent generations of wireless communication is poised to introduce a new era of connectivity, promising enhanced capabilities such as ultra-low latency, massive device density, and significantly higher data rates. However, this evolution also brings complex challenges regarding accountability, transparency, and trust. A primary challenge lies in the fact that 6G and beyond networks will likely be constructed by multiple providers utilizing shared infrastructure, which complicates the assurance of service quality and the attribution of responsibility for failures. To address these issues, this paper proposes a blockchain-based framework designed to ensure transparent and accountable network sharing. By leveraging the inherent transparency and immutability of blockchain technology, the proposed solution facilitates the creation of a secure, auditable, and verifiable record of network operations.

This study examines the two-dimensional dynamics of incompressible fluids within the context of the Okubo-Weiss criterion, a metric used to assess the relative significance of stretching versus shearing in fluid flows. We establish that the Okubo-Weiss criterion remains valid for both magnetohydrodynamics and hydrodynamics systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Okubo-Weiss criterion can be expressed as a transport equation, a formulation that facilitates the analysis of the evolution of two-dimensional fluid dynamics.

This study examines the thermodynamics of Lee-Wick (LW) fields within the cosmological context of the early universe. We demonstrate that the thermal behavior of LW fields is characterized by a thermal mass, which is essential for understanding their cosmological evolution. Furthermore, we analyze the cosmological evolution of LW fields, showing that the presence of LW fields can cause the universe to transition from a decelerating to an accelerating phase.

This paper introduces a novel transformer-based framework designed to address the challenge of image style transfer. By leveraging the self-attention mechanism, our approach effectively captures long-range dependencies, enabling the model to accurately map content features to style attributes. We employ a dual-transformer architecture, where one network processes the content image and the other handles the style image. This design allows for the precise alignment of corresponding content and style features. Furthermore, we integrate a multi-scale feature fusion module to enhance the model's ability to handle fine details. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in both visual quality and computational efficiency.

Thermodynamic length, defined as the geometric magnitude of a protocol's path within the space of equilibrium states, has been shown to establish a universal minimum for the dissipated work across all protocols sharing a fixed start and end state. This quantity is independent of the specific trajectory chosen and has been proven to be optimal for protocols with a constant rate of entropy production. In this study, we experimentally validate this principle using a single electron box, demonstrating that the constant-dissipation-rate protocol coincides with the thermodynamically optimal path.

This study examines the single production of a vector-like $T$ quark at a future high-energy linear $e^+e^-$ collider, focusing on the $T\bar{b}W$ model. We analyze the model's phenomenology, specifically investigating the $T$ quark's production and decay mechanisms. We evaluate the model's viability by comparing its predicted cross sections and decay branching ratios against current LHC limits. Furthermore, we calculate the signal-to-background ratio and projected statistical significance for the proposed $T\bar{b}W$ signal. Finally, we demonstrate that a future linear collider operating at a center-of-mass energy of 3 TeV could achieve a signal significance of 10.5$\sigma$ for the $T\bar{b}W$ process.

This study examines the stability of inhomogeneous fluids subjected to acoustic fields, utilizing the linearized Navier-Stokes equations to derive a dispersion relation for plane waves. The analysis reveals that inhomogeneous fluids in acoustic fields are generally unstable, with the exception of specific cases such as two-phase fluids where the density and compressibility ratios are constant. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the growth rate of these instabilities can be modulated by adjusting the acoustic pressure amplitude.

This study examines the analytic architecture of the powers of a weighted backward shift operating on generalized directed semi-trees. We establish that such an operator exhibits hypercyclicity, as well as properties of subhypercyclicity, suborbitally transitivity, and the existence of a dense orbit within the closed unit ball's boundary. Furthermore, we demonstrate the operator is not cyclical, does not possess supercyclic properties, and fails to be cospicy. Additionally, we prove the presence of a dense set of orbits that converge weakly to zero and establish the existence of a hypercyclic vector within a specific weighted $H^2$-space.

This study examines the generation of $\gamma$-photon flashes within the $\lambda^3$ regime, produced by an ultra-intense laser interacting with a solid target. The resulting $\gamma$-photon flash irradiates a high-Z target, triggering Compton scattering and the Breit-Wheeler process. We investigate the impact of the laser's intensity and pulse duration on the production of electron-positron pairs and radioactive nuclei. Our findings indicate that the $\gamma$-photon flash yields a significantly higher number of electron-positron pairs compared to those generated directly by the laser, while simultaneously producing a greater quantity of radioactive nuclei.

This study introduces a novel approach to event detection that leverages Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) combined with a specialized syntactic graph structure. The method employs a syntax-driven attention mechanism to weigh the significance of various dependency relations, while incorporating a gate diversity strategy to regulate information flow between the syntactic graph and the word embedding layer. We evaluate this model across three distinct datasets, demonstrating that it surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper establishes the geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers within a Bayesian error-in-variable regression framework. We rigorously prove that, under mild conditions, the sampler's Markov chain exhibits geometric convergence to the target distribution, regardless of the initial values used for the regression parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this theoretical result holds true in practical applications.

This study introduces a robust control method for interacting multi-qubit systems, specifically designed to sense weak magnetic fields. By employing a multi-step approach, we first determine the optimal control sequence for a single qubit, then extend this to two qubits using a fixed interaction Hamiltonian, and finally generalize the method to systems with three or more qubits. The approach is validated on a three-qubit system, where we demonstrate that the proposed control sequence successfully detects weak magnetic fields even in the presence of noise.

This study introduces a novel approach to nonlinear dynamical systems subject to random noise by employing a Krylov subspace. The method involves projecting the system onto a lower-dimensional space to generate a reduced-order model, which is then solved using the Krylov iteration. The resulting solutions are projected back to the original system space, where they are compared against the original system's behavior. The authors demonstrate that this strategy effectively captures the system's response to random noise. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of varying noise levels and the number of Krylov vectors on the solution. The method is validated through two examples: a Duffing oscillator and a Lorenz system.

This study examines wave propagation within scattering media characterized by nonlinear absorption. We develop a nonlinear radiative transport equation (RTE) to model intensity evolution in the diffusive regime, alongside a radiative transport order (RTO) equation for the transition regime. By deriving a nonlinear Schrödinger equation from these transport models, we establish a comprehensive framework linking them across varying regimes. Our analysis confirms that the nonlinear parameter in the derived Schrödinger equation is consistently consistent with the input parameter of the nonlinear absorption term in both the RTO and RTE formulations.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success across various domains, including game playing, robotics, and autonomous driving. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of these models has generated substantial concern regarding their explainability. This survey examines existing methods for explainable reinforcement learning, categorizing them into three groups: post-hoc explanation, model interpretability, and counterfactual explanation. We begin by outlining the fundamental concepts of RL and the key challenges associated with explaining these systems. Subsequently, we detail the specific techniques within each category, highlighting their advantages and limitations. Finally, we identify critical open issues and future research directions in the field of explainable RL.

This paper examines one-variable logics grounded in algebraic semantics, where the logic's language comprises formulas built from atomic variables and connectives that are either lattice-valued or take values in the lattice itself. We demonstrate that such logics can be characterized by a specific class of Kripke frames, notably extending the framework of Kripke semantics for one-variable modal logics. Furthermore, we establish that these logics are complete with respect to a broader class of algebraic semantics, defined as the variety of algebras generated by the algebraic models of the corresponding logic.

We establish the Wiener chaos decomposition of the stochastic exponential (Doléans-Dade exponential) associated with a Gaussian process, provided that the process' covariance function is analytic. This decomposition is expressed using multiple Wiener–Itô integrals, with the integrands defined as iterated integrals of the spectral measure. The methodology relies on the fact that the stochastic exponential's chaos expansion can be derived from the iterated Wiener–Itô integrals comprising its Taylor expansion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such expansions for the stochastic exponential of a Gaussian process naturally induce similar structures for the signatures of the process.

This study presents a statistical analysis of localization accuracy within millimeter-wave cellular networks, specifically focusing on time difference of arrival (TOA) and angle of arrival (AOA) techniques. For the TOA method, we derive a closed-form expression for the Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) regarding user position estimation, which incorporates the effects of path loss, shadowing, and beamforming. Furthermore, we evaluate the CRLB for the ARA technique and examine how the mean squared error (MSE) of the estimated location varies with the user's distance from the base station. Additionally, we analyze the CRLB associated with the estimated angle of arrival. Our findings indicate that the CRLB for the TOA-based approach is significantly lower than that for the ARA method, suggesting that TOA offers superior localization precision.

We examine a system of $N$ bosons confined in a volume $V$ at temperature $T$, where the chemical potential is fixed. Within the Gross-Pitaevskii limit defined by $N\to\infty$ and $N/V=const$, we demonstrate that the chemical potential converges to a finite value and that a fraction of the particles occupies a single quantum state.

This work builds upon a previous analysis by the same author, which established the existence of a ground state for the many-body wave function. That earlier result relied on the assumption that the particles are in a Bose-Einstein condensate, whereas the current study provides a rigorous proof of this very phenomenon.

The primary distinction between this paper and the prior one lies in the method of proof. Previously, the argument was constructed by first assuming the condensate's existence to derive a contradiction if it did not exist. In contrast, this paper employs a direct proof that derives the properties of a Bose-Einstein condensate from fundamental principles.

Image inpainting involves reconstructing missing or corrupted image regions by leveraging contextual information from the remainder of the image. This task is inherently difficult because the model must not only restore the missing pixels but also accurately infer the underlying scene geometry and semantic content. While recent deep learning approaches have achieved significant success in image restoration, they often struggle with high-resolution inputs due to the computational demands of processing vast amounts of data. To address this, we introduce a two-stage framework designed to handle high-resolution inpainting efficiently. The initial stage utilizes a deep learning model to generate a low-resolution inpainting result, which is then upsampled to a high resolution. In the second stage, a specialized inpainting network refines this upsampled image to produce the final output. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in both quantitative metrics and visual quality.

This study examines a problem-dependent perspective on bandit problems with structured thresholds. We introduce a novel algorithm, the Problem Dependent Upper Confidence Bound (PDUCB), which leverages problem-dependent gap information to achieve a regret rate of $\mathcal{O}(\log\log T)$. This bound represents a significant improvement over the standard $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ regret associated with conventional algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed PDUCB method is universally applicable across various problems featuring structured thresholds.

This article serves as an appendix to our work in the *Journal of the ACM* [1], where we demonstrated that the PSPACE-complete problem of verifying the succinctness of DPLL proofs for propositional satisfiability can be solved within polynomial time relative to the size of a provided DPLL refutation. We established that a DPLL refutation constitutes a succinct proof of unsatisfiability in the polynomial proof system (NP) for certain classes of formulas. In this addendum, we expand upon that result by showing that a DPLL refutation also constitutes a succinct proof of unsatisfiability within the coNP proof system (NP). We further prove that a DPLL refutation constitutes a succinct proof of unsatisfiability within the polynomial proof system (NP) for certain classes of formulas. We establish the existence of classical solutions to $H^\alpha$-flow for mean convex, complete n-hypersurfaces embedded in $(n+1)$-dimensional Euclidean space that initially assume a specific graph form. This methodology is further utilized to demonstrate the existence of expanding solutions for the same flow under graph assumptions.

We derive a sum rule for fluctuations of vortex pairs in a two-dimensional superfluid by utilizing the Coulomb gas framework. This rule demonstrates that the long-range behavior of the vortex-pair correlation function is governed by the screening length, which is determined by the ratio of the pair fugacity to the superfluid density. Furthermore, we establish that these pair correlations decay algebraically with distance, with the exponent linked to the screening length exponent, and we provide an explicit formula for this exponent.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming a ubiquitous part of daily life, yet public comprehension of its capabilities and risks remains limited. This study examines how people perceive AI, specifically focusing on their knowledge levels, excitement regarding its future, and concerns about potential dangers. Utilizing data from a large-scale international survey conducted across eight nations, we analyzed responses from 1,000 participants in each country. Our findings reveal that while individuals possess a moderate understanding of current AI applications, they are significantly less optimistic about future developments. The data indicates that public perception is heavily influenced by demographic variables, including age, education, and gender. Furthermore, we observed that respondents in the United States and the United Kingdom hold more positive outlooks on AI than their counterparts in the other surveyed countries. These results highlight the critical need for targeted public engagement strategies to foster a more nuanced and informed dialogue concerning the opportunities and risks associated with artificial intelligence.

The analysis presents the first-ever measurement of the branching fraction for the Cabibbo-suppressed decay $\Xi_c^0\to \pi^-\Lambda_c^+$, utilizing data from LHCb's 2016 proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The branching fraction is determined to be $\mathcal{B}(\Xi_c^0\to \pi^-\Lambda_c^+) = (1.01 \pm 0.12 \pm 0.07) \times 10^{-3}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic.

This paper introduces several new fixed point theorems regarding products of two operators within Banach algebras. We also examine a specific class of functional equations, formulating both necessary and sufficient conditions to ensure the existence of solutions. Additionally, we establish both approximation and nonapproximability criteria for the solution set of these equations. Our findings rely on the spectral radius of the product of two operators, along with the real and complex spectra of constituent operators. Furthermore, we provide concrete examples to illustrate the derived results.

Actor-Critic (AC) reinforcement learning has proven highly effective for solving complex tasks, yet it remains susceptible to local optima and hyperparameter tuning. This study introduces a novel AC framework that integrates Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) to enhance both sample efficiency and training stability. By employing HMC to generate correlated samples from a Gaussian distribution, the method optimizes the actor's policy parameters. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm and demonstrate its convergence to the optimal policy under specific conditions. Empirical results across multiple environments indicate that the new approach outperforms standard AC methods in terms of both training stability and final performance.

We investigate the Dicke model, which describes a system of interacting bosonic modes and spins, within a triangular lattice configuration. By analyzing the system's phase diagram, we identify a region where three phases coexist, known as tricriticality. This tricritical point is characterized by a unique chiral quantum phase that breaks time-reversal symmetry and exhibits broken degeneracy between the two bosonic modes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this tricritical point can be converted into a quantum phase transition by adjusting the interaction strength.

Transfer learning (TL) offers a promising approach to accelerate the training of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policies by leveraging knowledge from a source domain. However, existing TL methods often fail to adapt to the specific characteristics of different domains, leading to performance degradation in some cases. To address this, we introduce Level-Adaptive Credit Assignment (LACA), a novel framework for domain-invariant policy transfer. LACA operates by first identifying a high-performing policy within the source domain and then dynamically adjusting its parameters to align with the target domain's requirements. This adjustment process utilizes a hierarchical credit assignment mechanism that assigns responsibility for performance to both individual agents and the collective group. By integrating these two levels, LACA effectively balances the contributions of agents and the group, thereby mitigating the negative transfer phenomenon. Empirical evaluations across three demanding MARL tasks demonstrate that LACA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art transfer learning approaches.

Particle-based systems are increasingly utilized in robotics for their adaptability and capacity to model complex physical phenomena. However, the absence of suitable simulation environments hinders the use of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for training robotic agents within this domain. This paper introduces a novel, high-fidelity 2D simulation environment designed to support DRL training for robotic tasks involving particle robots. The environment features a custom physics engine that accurately captures interactions between particles and external forces, as well as between particles themselves. We validate the environment's efficacy by training a robotic arm to navigate a particle robot through a maze and to relocate the robot to specific target locations. Additionally, we demonstrate the system's utility in learning control strategies for manipulating particle clusters to achieve specific configurations.

We report the detection of a 3-sigma upper limit on potassium absorption in the atmosphere of the hot Jupiter WASP-31b. This finding stems from a transit observation conducted on 2018 April 10 using the 2.6-meter telescope at the Teide Observatory in Tenerife, which utilized a custom-built, high-resolution echelle spectrograph. The data were analyzed using the Bayesian retrieval framework, which yielded a 3-sigma upper limit on the potassium absorption feature of 1.5% at the 95% confidence level. This constraint is consistent with prior observations of WASP-31b by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Keck II telescope. Consequently, we conclude that WASP-31b lacks detectable potassium in its atmosphere.

Cloud High-Performance Computing-as-a-Service (HPCaaS) is becoming increasingly popular, yet it currently faces significant hurdles, including the need to rapidly scale compute power, manage data transfer, and minimize operational expenses. This paper introduces a novel architecture for HPCaaS that leverages Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) to address these issues. By utilizing NVM, the system can instantly scale resources and maintain data persistence across shutdowns, enabling rapid task resumption. We present a comprehensive analysis of the architecture's design, performance, and cost-effectiveness, supported by a prototype implementation. Experimental results indicate that this NVM-based approach achieves up to a 100x improvement in startup latency and a 10x increase in throughput compared to conventional cloud HPC solutions.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a non-invasive neuroimaging technique that maps brain activity by detecting hemodynamic changes. In recent years, fMRI has gained significant attention for its potential in diagnosing neurological disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, fMRI data presents unique challenges: it is high-dimensional, noisy, and suffers from low inter-subject variability. To address these issues, we introduce a novel contrastive graph learning framework designed to leverage the strengths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and contrastive learning. This approach first constructs a graph for each individual using GNNs, then employs contrastive learning to generate graph representations that are both discriminative and robust to noise. Experimental results on an fMRI dataset from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper explores the Gauss sum $\tau$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, where $q = p^f$ ($q$ is a prime power), with $q$ being the field size and $p$ the characteristic prime. We establish that $\tau$ serves as a fundamental invariant for the field $\mathbb{F}_q$, demonstrating that it uniquely determines the field's size. Furthermore, we examine the arithmetic properties of $\tau$ and its connection to the Frobenius automorphism, revealing that $\tau$ acts as a natural generalization of the quadratic residue symbol. We also explore the interplay between $\tau$ and the structure of the field's multiplicative group, showing that $\tau$ can be used to construct a basis for the field as a vector space over its prime subfield. Finally, we discuss the role of $\tau$ in determining the field's arithmetic structure, demonstrating that $\tau$ can be used to recover the field's characteristic prime $p$ and the exponent $f$ in the expression $q = p^f$.

This study reports the experimental observation of Cherenkov radiation in the soft X-ray spectrum, generated by 1.5 MeV electrons traversing thin beryllium and silicon foils. The investigation utilized a synchrotron radiation beamline at the BESSY II facility in Berlin, Germany. The experimental findings align well with theoretical calculations.

The Universal Conceptual Depiction (UCCA) framework models semantic relationships between entities, such as those found in "John ate the apple," through a graph connecting nodes representing these entities. In this structure, nodes are categorized by their roles, including Agent, Theme, and Source. While nodes for explicit mentions like "John" and "apple" are straightforward, representing concepts that are implicit—such as "eating" or "the act of"—poses a significant challenge. To address this, we introduce a refined annotation scheme that represents implicit concepts as action verbs. This approach offers two key advantages: first, it aligns with existing linguistic annotation standards, and second, it enables the reuse of established natural language processing techniques for Universal Conceptual Depiction tasks. We detail our annotation methodology, present evaluation metrics, and share preliminary results from a pilot study involving 1,000 sentences.

This study introduces a self-guided multiple instance learning (MIL) framework designed for weakly supervised disease classification and localization in chest X-rays. The method employs a dual-branch architecture: a main branch generates the global image label, while a sub-branch produces self-generated weak supervision signals. These signals are then utilized to train the primary classifier. To ensure the sub-branch remains robust, we implement a self-guided training strategy that enforces consistency between the sub-branch's outputs and the main-branch predictions. Furthermore, we integrate a novel attention-based MIL model to achieve precise localization. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both classification accuracy and localization performance.

We introduce a new model selection criterion grounded in penalized Hellinger distance, designed to address the limitations of existing methods that often perform poorly in small samples. By employing a penalty term derived from the expected Hellinger distance, we ensure that selected models are those with the minimum adjusted distance to the true underlying model. The proposed approach is validated through a simulation study, demonstrating its superior performance over AIC, BIC, and the widely used Shibata's information criterion (SIC) in model selection tasks.

We demonstrate that for any given binary pattern, the number of occurrences within the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence can be precisely calculated using a number-theoretic formula. Furthermore, we establish that any given binary pattern appears infinitely often as a subsequence within the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence.

This study introduces a cost-sensitive hierarchical clustering approach designed for dynamic classifier selection (DCS). The proposed method identifies the most effective classifiers for each specific data subset by grouping them based on performance metrics and correlation coefficients. The DCS strategy is then employed to determine an optimal weighting scheme for these clusters, enabling the selection of a weighted combination of datasets rather than relying on a single best classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed DCS method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of classification accuracy.

The Tianlai project, a low-frequency radio telescope network situated in the Yangzhou region of Jiangsu Province, China, is designed to investigate the Epoch of Reionization and the 21-cm signal from the Dark Ages. This paper details the data processing workflow for Tianlai, covering the stages from raw data acquisition to the generation of power spectra.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, we investigate the magnetic characteristics of the recently discovered monolayer materials NbSi2N4, VSi2P4, and VSi2P4. Our findings reveal that NbSi2N4 and VSi2P4 monolayers exhibit robust antiferromagnetic (AFM) ground states, whereas VSi2P4 displays a ferromagnetic (FM) ground state. Additionally, the AFM-to-FM phase transition in VSi2P4 is found to be first-order. The calculated magnetic anisotropy energies (MAE) for these monolayers are exceptionally high, reaching approximately 1.0 meV per magnetic moment for NbSi2N4 and 0.2 meV per magnetic moment for VSi2P4. These results indicate that the monolayer materials NbSi2N4 and VSi2P4 are promising candidates for spintronic applications.

This study introduces a novel technique for constructing positive definite functions on ordered sets, extending the classic Gneiting approach originally designed for Euclidean spaces. We demonstrate that this method encompasses previous strategies for building such functions on both Euclidean spaces and metric spaces.

A monoid is defined as atomic when it can be constructed by combining indecomposable elements, and it is classified as atomic positive if it can be represented as the closure of its own positive elements under this property. This paper demonstrates that all atomic positive monoids are indeed atomic. Furthermore, we establish that the class of atomic positive monoids is closed under direct products and subsemigroups formed by taking isomorphic copies. Finally, we prove that every finitely generated free commutative monoid possesses atomic properties.

The attributable fraction among the exposed (AFex) quantifies the proportion of disease occurrences in an exposed group that can be attributed to the exposure itself. While widely utilized in epidemiology, AFex estimation typically relies on exposure and outcome data, which are often subject to bias. This paper introduces a novel framework that leverages case description details to diminish AFex's sensitivity to such biases. We demonstrate that this approach is applicable to various bias types, including those arising from measurement errors, missing data, and confounding. Furthermore, we establish that the AFex estimator derived from this method is consistent and asymptotically normal. The AFex's variance is estimated using the bootstrap technique, and its performance is validated through simulations. Finally, the proposed methodology is applied to assess the impact of air pollution on mortality in the New York City area.

This work examines zero-cycles on normal projective varieties, specifically focusing on those that are quasi-projective. We demonstrate that for any such normal quasi-projective variety, there exists a projective subvariety within the same class of zero-cycles. Furthermore, we establish a condition regarding the normality of a variety based on the properties of its zero-cycles. Additionally, we explore the connection between the Chow group of zero-cycles and the Albanese map, and we provide a sufficient condition for a projective variety to possess a rational point.

This study examines the event-activity dependence of $\Upsilon$(nS) ($n=1,2,3$) relative production within the central pseudorapidity range $|\eta|<0.8$ for the $\Upsilon$(nS) and its daughter pions, utilizing the LHCb detector at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV. The analysis focuses on the ratio of $\Upsilon$(nS) production to that of $\Upsilon$(1S) as a function of charged-particle multiplicity density. The findings indicate that the ratio of $\Upsilon$(2S)/$\Upsilon$(1S) production decreases with increasing charged-particle multiplicity density, whereas the ratio of $\Upsilon$(3S)/$\Upsilon$(1S) production remains constant. These results are compared against theoretical predictions derived from the Color Glass Condensate model and the Color Evaporation Model.

We introduce a novel method for measuring the entropy of a quantum dot by utilizing the absorption of infrared radiation by an attached phononic crystal. This technique relies on the interaction between the dot and the crystal's phononic modes, which are engineered to be strongly coupled. The resulting changes in the crystal's optical response allow for the determination of the dot's entropy.

This paper introduces a non-negative real-valued function, termed the geometric modulus, which serves as a generalization of the geometric radius introduced by A. L. Edrei and W. K. Hayman. This geometric modulus is defined as the infimum of the radii of open disks centered at a specific point $z_0$ that are free of zeros for a given holomorphic function. The geometric radius was originally defined to demonstrate that a holomorphic function with a non-vanishing derivative possesses at most one simple zero within a simply connected domain. In this study, we extend the definition of the geometric radius to apply to both holomorphic and harmonic functions that may have multiple zeros. Furthermore, we establish a new analytic result concerning the uniqueness of solutions to a particular class of differential equations.

This study examines the stability of discrete nonlinear Schrödinger (DNLS) solitons within a one-dimensional lattice featuring dipole-dipole interactions. The analysis reveals that these solitons are susceptible to both modulational and modulational-like instabilities, which are driven by the nonpolynomial character of the nonlinearity. Furthermore, the presence of dipole-dipole interactions induces a collapse phenomenon, which is investigated through numerical simulations. These simulations demonstrate that the collapse manifests as a self-focusing process in the discrete domain, resulting in the formation of a localized state on a single site.

This study introduces a new algorithm for solving signomial programming problems, a category of non-convex optimization tasks that encompasses geometric programming as a specific instance. The method leverages a novel transformation of the objective function alongside a majorization-minimization framework. We establish that this algorithm converges to a stationary point and demonstrate its finite termination when applied to signomial programs. Furthermore, the approach is adaptable to various constraints, including linear, convex, and specific nonlinear types. Numerical experiments indicate that the proposed algorithm achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.

This survey explores the interplay between ergodic theory and Teichmuller theory, with a specific focus on recent developments regarding unimodular representations of surface groups. It also provides a brief review of the classical Torelli theorem for hyperbolic curves and discusses the emerging global Torelli theorem for unmarked Teichmuller spaces.

We introduce a method for creating personalized neural avatars from a solitary RGB-D video sequence. Our approach utilizes a convolutional neural network to extract person-specific features, which are then integrated with a generic model of human body dynamics to generate an implicit representation of the individual. This strategy enables the reconstruction of neural avatars for new subjects without the need for labor-intensive manual annotations. Furthermore, the avatars facilitate high-fidelity rendering of novel viewpoints and support applications such as motion transfer and virtual reality.

This study introduces a new method for addressing face de-occlusion, a task that reconstructs occluded facial regions. The approach utilizes a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) to generate a 3D face mesh, which is then projected into 2D space to create a depth map. This depth map guides the generative process of a GAN to synthesize the missing facial areas. The system was trained on the CelebA-Haze dataset and evaluated using the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) metric. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Intrinsically Motivated Reinforcement Learning (IMRL) is a subfield of Reinforcement Learning (RL) that has gained significant attention recently. This field aims to develop autonomous agents capable of learning complex behaviors without relying on external rewards. By utilizing intrinsic motivation, IMRL enables agents to autonomously set goals, thereby enhancing their ability to learn from sparse rewards and tackle difficult tasks. This paper provides a concise overview of IMRL, covering its foundational concepts, primary methodologies, and associated challenges.

This paper introduces a Localized Policy Iteration (LPI) algorithm designed for networked multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents optimize their individual policies using only local information. We demonstrate that the LPI algorithm achieves global convergence to a locally Nash equilibrium within a general framework of single-step discounted games. Furthermore, we establish that the algorithm exhibits linear convergence when applied to two specific classes of two-player networked games. Our findings are validated through numerical experiments.

This study examines dijet events characterized by a substantial rapidity gap between the two leading jets, utilizing proton-proton collision data from the CMS detector at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The dataset comprises an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$, recorded during the 2010 run. The analysis specifically targets events where the leading jet transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) exceeds 100 GeV and the second leading jet $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ is greater than 20 GeV. The observed production cross section for these dijet events is measured to be 1.1 $\pm$ 0.2 (stat.) $\pm$ 0.2 (syst.) nb. Additionally, the distribution of the rapidity gap is analyzed, and the findings are compared against predictions from both next-to-leading order QCD calculations and Monte Carlo simulations.

This study investigates the thermoelectric properties of penta-silicene, a newly identified two-dimensional material. Our findings indicate that its electronic band structure features a direct bandgap of 0.31 eV, situated at the $\Gamma$ point, alongside a direct valence band maximum at the $\Gamma$ point. Consequently, penta-silicene exhibits a direct bandgap nature, which is advantageous for thermoelectric applications. Furthermore, its electronic and thermal transport characteristics demonstrate significant potential for thermoelectric use, particularly at room temperature. Specifically, the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity is negligible, a feature that enhances its thermoelectric performance. Additionally, the material possesses a high Seebeck coefficient and a large effective mass, which are critical factors for optimizing thermoelectric efficiency. These attributes collectively suggest that penta-silicene is a promising candidate for thermoelectric devices operating at room temperature.

This study investigates the spectra of heavy quarkonia within a magnetized hot medium using a non-relativistic fractional framework. We employ the fractional Schrödinger equation to derive the ground state energy and wave function for the $1S$ state of charmonium and bottomonium, incorporating a Cornell potential alongside a Debye screening potential. Our findings indicate that the ground state energy and the radius of the $1S$ state for both systems are sensitive to variations in the fractional parameter $\alpha$. Furthermore, we examine the effects of temperature and external magnetic field strength on these spectral properties. We find that the radius of the $1S$ state increases with higher temperatures and magnetic field strengths, whereas the energy decreases under the same conditions. Additionally, we observe that the radius of the $1S$ state is smaller for bottomonium than for charmonium.

This study examines the scattering of dark matter (DM) by subhalos, specifically focusing on the subhalo-to-halo mass ratio ($f_{\rm SH}$) and the resulting DM density profiles. We demonstrate that subhalos can significantly alter the DM density distribution within host halos, particularly in the central regions, thereby affecting the DM mass fraction ($f_{\rm SH}$) and the central density profile. We also explore the implications of these findings for direct detection experiments and the interpretation of astrophysical observations.

This study examines the joint optimization of allocation and patrolling within a signaling game featuring an intelligent adversary, where the defender must assign resources to patrol locations and the adversary must choose targets to attack. The problem is further complicated by uncertainty regarding the adversary's specific objectives and the potential outcomes of attacks. We demonstrate that the defender's strategy can be modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and solved using reinforcement learning (RL). Additionally, we introduce a novel approach to estimate the adversary's objective, which is proven to be equivalent to a specific MDP. We also develop a specialized algorithm to handle the computational challenges inherent in solving this MDP. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed method through a case study involving a network of maritime patrol aircraft.

This paper introduces a deep reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed to enable robots to navigate uneven outdoor terrains. The system employs a novel approach that integrates a learned RL policy with a probabilistic terrain elevation model (TERP), allowing the robot to generate a sequence of terrain-specific policies and execute them sequentially. This method ensures robustness against terrain uncertainties and significantly outperforms existing RL techniques in both reliability and generalization. Experimental results demonstrate that TERP successfully navigates complex, previously unseen environments with high reliability.

This study examines the phase diagram of a three-dimensional system featuring dipolar interactions alongside short-range repulsive forces, utilizing both Monte Carlo simulations and variational approaches. The analysis reveals that the transition from a normal state to a superfluid occurs via a first-order phase change, which terminates at a critical point. Furthermore, the system exhibits a distinct normal-to-disordered transition that is of first order and ends at a critical endpoint.

This study investigates an inverse problem involving a planar conductive inclusion. We demonstrate that the inclusion's geometry can be uniquely determined from the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, provided certain conditions are met. Furthermore, we present a novel, data-driven method for reconstructing the inclusion. This approach utilizes a specific family of Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps to generate an efficient iterative algorithm capable of recovering the inclusion's geometry.

We examine the stability of axially symmetric magnetic fields within stellar environments, specifically focusing on the poloidal component. Our analysis demonstrates that any stable poloidal field must be either a dipole or a quadrupole field. Furthermore, we establish that the poloidal field is stable only if the magnetic energy density is sufficiently low.

This study examines the geometric and topological attributes of simplicial synchronization within networked dynamical systems. Specifically, we investigate the topological organization of simplicial synchronization manifolds, demonstrating that the set of such manifolds forms a stratified space. We further establish that the stratification of these manifolds is governed by the combinatorial properties of the underlying simplicial graph. Additionally, we analyze the homotopy and homology groups of these spaces, revealing that their homotopy groups are trivial and that homology groups are concentrated exclusively in the zeroth dimension. Finally, we provide numerical simulations to validate these theoretical findings.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) serves as a foundational operation in numerous scientific and engineering applications, including iterative solvers for linear systems, graph algorithms, and finite element analysis. This paper introduces a suite of performance enhancement strategies for SpMV, specifically targeting the challenges of irregular data access and high memory bandwidth requirements. We present a new SpMV implementation that leverages data locality and prefetching to mitigate irregular access, alongside an iterative solver that employs tiling to reduce bandwidth demands. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining these techniques yields significant performance gains. We validate our findings using a high-performance computing cluster equipped with Intel Xeon Phi coprocessors, showing that the proposed methods achieve up to a 1.5x speedup in SpMV and a 1.3x speedup in iterative solvers.

This study investigates a second-order linear difference meromorphic equation defined over the complex plane, where the coefficient functions are also meromorphic. The equation's entire right-hand side is derived from a product of two distinct meromorphic functions, $f$ and $g$, which are themselves not constants. The work establishes specific conditions ensuring that normality with respect to $f$ implies normality with respect to $g$. Furthermore, these findings are extended to cases involving shifted meromorphic functions.

This paper introduces a novel system for intention recognition in head-mounted augmented reality (AR) environments, designed to address the unique challenges posed by AR's extended depth of field. By leveraging both human and environmental cues, our approach enables AR wearers to anticipate the intentions of others, thereby enhancing collaboration and communication. We detail a system that captures and processes these signals, and through a user study, we validate that our system successfully infers intentions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical value of this technology by implementing it within a collaborative AR scenario.

We examine the variational characteristics of Monge-Ampère systems defined over a manifold of dimension $2n+2$ that admit a Lagrangian pair. Specifically, we establish that every such system possesses a Hamiltonian formulation involving $n$ degrees of freedom and a variational complex structured as a first-order system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associated Euler-Lagrange equations reduce to a set of quasi-linear second-order partial differential equations. Finally, we explore the link between these systems and contact geometry, proving that any system admitting both a Lagrangian pair and a contact structure can be expressed via a generalized generating function.

This study investigates the impact of buoyancy-driven convection on the growth and dissolution of bubbles at an electrode within a liquid electrolyte. By employing a two-dimensional model that accounts for both convection and diffusion, we analyzed the evolution of the bubble's shape and the surrounding concentration field. The analysis reveals that convection significantly alters bubble growth and dissolution dynamics, with the extent of this influence depending on the bubble's size, its distance from the electrode, and the system's Rayleigh number.

This study presents a search for long-lived particles (LLPs) that decay into photons within the CMS detector at the CERN LHC. Utilizing 2018 proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 135 fb$^{-1}$ at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, the analysis examines scenarios where LLPs originate from the interaction point and decay into photons either inside or beyond the detector. The results show no significant deviation from Standard Model predictions, establishing 95% confidence level upper limits on the production cross-section multiplied by the branching fraction. These constraints apply across various LLP masses ranging from 10 to 1000 GeV and decay lengths extending from 10 cm to 1000 m.

We investigate the impact of Coulomb interactions on the second-order Dirac semimetal (SODSM) within the $d$-$p$ model, which features a four-fold degenerate band structure. Our analysis reveals that the system undergoes a transition from a semimetallic to a correlated insulating state, driven by the formation of a charge-density wave (CDW) phase. This phase is characterized by a gap opening in the semimetallic bands and a reduction in the Dirac cone's linear dispersion. Furthermore, we observe that the CDW transition temperature is highly sensitive to the interaction strength, exhibiting a non-monotonic dependence on the hopping parameter.

This paper introduces a method for automatically synthesizing data structure implementations, specifically targeting concurrent linked lists. By employing Answer Set Programming (ASP) to derive the necessary update rules, the approach generates code that adheres to specified invariants. The process involves modeling a linked list as a collection of nodes and encoding these updates as a set of logic rules within an ASP program. This program utilizes the "node" predicate to represent the structure, ensuring that any solution logically satisfies the defined invariants. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method by applying it to the three primary operations on a concurrent linked list: concurrent push, concurrent pop, and mixed push/pop.

We introduce a novel experimental method for detecting deviations from standard gravity by measuring the resonant frequency of a test mass within a magnetically levitated resonator. This approach offers a distinct advantage over traditional torsion balance experiments because it allows for the precise, real-time monitoring of the test mass's position. We demonstrate that these capabilities enable the detection of minute anomalous forces, thereby permitting a stringent test of gravitational laws at sub-millimeter scales.

We report the detection of two isomers of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (cyclopentadiene with a CCH group) in the TMC-1 molecular cloud: 1-ethynyl cyclopentadiene (1-EPD) and 2-ethynyl cyclopentadiene (2-EPD). Using the IRAM 30m telescope, we identified 1-EPD through the rotational transition J = 11–10 at 115.27 GHz and 2-EPD via its J = 11–10 transition at 115.27 GHz. The observed column densities are $1.0 \times 10^{11}$ cm$^{-2}$ for 1-EPD and $1.0 \times 10^{11}$ cm$^{-2}$ for 2-EPD, respectively. These findings represent the first detection of ethynyl cyclopentadiene and the first observation of a substituted cyclopentadiene in the interstellar medium. The abundance ratio of 1-EPD to 2-EPD is approximately 1.0, which aligns with the statistical expectation of 1.0.
